requirements.nl_text: Request Number - 328 | Request Title - Feature request: Sending dummy short messages | Request Description - TextSecure could mask meaningful communication between people by occasionally sending dummy random messages to random recipients at random times:  Recipients would be chosen randomly between contacts that knowingly use TextSecure, so it could be recognized as such after decryption and automatically discarded by recipient. "Randomness" should be tweaked to level-out the legitimate messages, spoiling the traffic analysis of traffic retention data, preventing to weigh connections in the deducted social network graph or guessing sleeping/activity patterns. People often have many unused messages in their monthly quota, so those could easily be used with no extra cost, or they value their privacy more than some money. Sender would need to enable this feature (opt-in) and define desired quantity (eg max 100 dummy messages per month, 2 dummy messages for every legitimate one, max 500 messages total counting legitimate and dummy ones...). The feature would need to be aware of roaming (disabled by default, optionally enable) and battery level (do not send if bellow eg. 30%). http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traffic_analysis#Countermeasures Possible extensions:  Recipients could be able to let their peers know, that they do not want to participate in this and do not want to receive messages for whatever reason (opt-out). Recipients could also be chosen randomly between other contacts (those not using TextSecure yet) to promote its use (default message) or a custom explanation by sender. verdict.text:
A caveat comes first. The study context says non-atomic requirements were excluded, but this run does not match that. It is the blind task, and the gold contains 15 non-atomic requirements: 77 units across 50 requests, including 328-Signal with 5 units and 802-Signal with 6. Either the wrong gold file was used or the filter was not applied. The unit results below are real, but this run is not the "easier atomic subset" described.

Track 1 is dominated by a convention mismatch rather than by fabrication. Actor and modalVerb show near-perfect recall but precision of 0.03 and 0.02, because there is almost nothing genuinely missing to detect: support is 1 for each. The real behaviour is in the implied rows. The model emitted `<MISSING_ACTOR> <MISSING_MODAL_VERB>` for 62 of 76 implied modal verbs (see 4031-Signal and 496-Signal), where annotators write "the App must". Under CoT the model takes a strictly literal reading. That is defensible, but it is not the gold convention.

The scope and condition numbers look like silent filling (46 and 19 cases). The examples suggest a parser artifact instead. 4031-Signal and 496-Signal contain no scope or condition at all, yet are scored "filled". The model simply omitted the `<MISSING_SCOPE>, <MISSING_CONDITION>` prefix that humans include, and absence is being read as filling. Until the parser treats an omitted slot as missing, the 0.41 flag rate is not interpretable.

The one genuine fabrication signal is action. All 4 gold-missing actions were filled: 83-, 496-, 592- and 1504-Signal. Each is a title-only request where the model turned the title into a requirement. With n=4, and annotators split on 1504-Signal (one of three wrote an action), this is suggestive, not conclusive.

On similarity, mean seq_ratio is 0.57 against a human-human ceiling of 0.72, and Jaccard is 0.39 against 0.55, roughly 70–80% of the ceiling. Part of that gap is mechanical: placeholder tokens in place of "the App must" and the missing scope/condition prefix both lower string overlap without any difference in meaning. The cosine figure (n=3, all zeros) and the absent embeddings should be ignored.

Paska's 14% pass rate largely measures the same placeholder habit. Paska cannot recognise a system response that begins `<MISSING_ACTOR> <MISSING_MODAL_VERB>`, which yields the 36 "Not requirement" and 25 "modal verb missing" smells. Outputs the model marked complete pass at 70%, while incomplete ones pass at 6%. That split shows the smells track the placeholder convention more than actual requirement quality.

Unit handling shows high-recall, over-eager splitting. Non-atomic detection recall is 14 of 15, but 7 atomic requests were split, including 6077-, 7345- and 2055-Signal into 3 each. Total output was 114 units against 77, and 328-Signal produced 19 against 5. 6390-Signal went the other way: it was under-split, and its first unit came back empty (similarity 0, Paska error).

The most useful next step is to fix the measurement before comparing strategies. Score an omitted scope or condition as missing. Then either tell the model that "the App"/"must" count as implied defaults, or normalise them in post-processing. Re-run Paska and similarity after that. Separately, check why non-atomic items are in this set, and inspect the four title-only cases by hand.
